'''Pierre Laurent Wantzel''' (5 June 1814 – 21 May 1848) was a French [[mathematician]] who proved that several ancient [[geometry|geometric]] problems were impossible to solve using only [[compass and straightedge]].<ref name = "Cajori">{{cite journal|author=Cajori, Florian|title=Pierre Laurent Wantzel|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1918|volume=24|issue=7|pages=339–347|mr=1560082|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1918-03088-7|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In a paper from 1837,<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Wantzel |first=L. |date=1837 |title=Recherches sur les moyens de reconnaître si un Problème de Géométrie peut se résoudre avec la règle et le compas |trans-title=Investigations into means of knowing if a problem of geometry can be solved with a straightedge and compass |url=https://www.numdam.org/item/JMPA_1837_1_2__366_0.pdf |journal=[[Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées]] |series=1 |language=fr |volume=2 |pages=366–372 |via={{Ill|NUMDAM|fr|Numérisation de documents anciens mathématiques}}}}</ref> Wantzel proved that the problems of [[doubling the cube]] and [[trisecting the angle]] are impossible to solve if one uses only a [[compass and straightedge]]. In the same paper he also solved the problem of determining which [[constructible polygon|regular polygons are constructible]]: a regular polygon is constructible [[if and only if]] the number of its sides is the product of a [[power of two]] and any number of distinct [[Fermat prime]]s (i.e., the sufficient conditions given by [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] are also necessary).

The solution to these problems had been sought for thousands of years, particularly by the ancient Greeks. However, Wantzel's work was neglected by his contemporaries, being virtually uncelebrated at the time of publishing,<ref name=":0" /> and was essentially forgotten. Indeed, it was only 50 years after its publication that Wantzel's article was mentioned either in a journal article<ref name=":2">{{Citation|last = Echegaray|first = José|author-link = José Echegaray|journal = Revista de los Progresos de las Ciencias Exactas, Físicas y Naturales|volume = 22|pages = 1–47|title = Metodo de Wantzel para conocer si un problema puede resolverse con la recta y el circulo|language = Spanish|year = 1887}}</ref> or in a textbook.<ref>{{Citation|last = Echegaray|first = José|author-link = José Echegaray|title = Disertaciones matemáticas sobre la cuadratura del círculo: El metodo de Wantzel y la división de la circunferencia en partes iguales|publisher = Imprenta de la Viuda é Hijo de D. E. Aguado|year = 1887|url = http://rodin.uca.es/xmlui/bitstream/handle/10498/7163/33925574.pdf|access-date = 15 May 2016|language = Spanish|archive-date = 4 June 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160604190840/http://rodin.uca.es/xmlui/bitstream/handle/10498/7163/33925574.pdf|url-status = dead}}</ref> Before that, it seems to have been mentioned only once, by [[Julius Petersen]], in his doctoral thesis of 1871. It was probably due to an article published about Wantzel by [[Florian Cajori]] more than 80 years after the publication of Wantzel's article<ref name="Cajori"/> that his name started to be well known among mathematicians.<ref>{{Citation|last = Lützen|first = Jesper|title = Why was Wantzel overlooked for a century? The changing importance of an impossibility result|journal = [[Historia Mathematica]]|year = 2009|volume = 36|issue = 4|pages = 374–394|doi = 10.1016/j.hm.2009.03.001|doi-access = }}</ref>

Wantzel was also the first person to prove, in 1843,<ref>{{Citation|last = Wantzel|first = [[Monsieur|M.]] L.|url = http://archive.numdam.org/ARCHIVE/NAM/NAM_1843_1_2_/NAM_1843_1_2__117_1/NAM_1843_1_2__117_1.pdf|title = Classification des nombres incommensurables d'origine algébrique|journal = [[Nouvelles Annales de Mathématiques]]|year = 1843|volume = 2|pages = 117–127|language = french}}</ref> that if a cubic polynomial with rational coefficients has three real roots but is irreducible in {{math|'''Q'''[''x'']}} (the so-called ''[[casus irreducibilis]]''), then the roots cannot be expressed from the coefficients using real radicals alone; that is, complex non-real numbers must be involved if one expresses the roots from the coefficients using radicals. This theorem would be rediscovered decades later by (and sometimes attributed to) [[Vincenzo Mollame]] and [[Otto Hölder]].

{{cquote
|quote = Ordinarily he worked evenings, not lying down until late; then he read, and took only a few hours of troubled sleep, making alternately wrong use of coffee and opium, and taking his meals at irregular hours until he was married.  He put unlimited trust in his constitution, very strong by nature, which he taunted at pleasure by all sorts of abuse. He brought sadness to those who mourn his premature death.
|author = [[Adhémar Jean Claude Barré de Saint-Venant]], on the occasion of Wantzel's death.<ref name="Cajori"/>
}}

Wantzel is often overlooked for his contributions to mathematics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lützen |first=Jesper |date=2009-11-01 |title=Why was Wantzel overlooked for a century? The changing importance of an impossibility result |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S031508600900010X |journal=Historia Mathematica |volume=36 |issue=4 |pages=374–394 |doi=10.1016/j.hm.2009.03.001 |issn=0315-0860|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In fact, for over a century there was great confusion as to who proved the impossibility theorems.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Richeson |first1=David S. |chapter=TANGENT: Nine Impossibility Theorems |pages=34–37 |doi=10.2307/j.ctvfrxrpr.8 |jstor=j.ctvfrxrpr.8 |title=Tales of Impossibility: The 2000-Year Quest to Solve the Mathematical Problems of Antiquity |date=2019 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-19296-3 }}</ref>

Wantzel died at just 33 years old, which historical accounts attribute to an overuse of [[caffeine]], [[opium]], and [[occupational burnout]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />
